    {
      "name": "Young Cabbage, Sprouts",
      "photo_filename": null,
      "servings": null,
      "prep_time": null,

        "SPROUTS",

        "PEPPER",
        "LOVAGE",
        "MINT",
        "RUE",
        "CORIANDER",
        "TENDER LEAVES OF THE STALKS",
        "BROTH"
      ],
      "directions": [
        "Boil the SPROUTS; season with CUMIN, SALT, WINE AND OIL; IF YOU LIKE add PEPPER, LOVAGE, MINT, RUE, CORIANDER; THE TENDER LEAVES OF THE STALKS stew IN BROTH; WINE AND OIL BE THE SEASONING."
      ],
      "notes": "Including, perhaps, cauliflower and broccoli. Served sometimes raw with dressing, sometimes boiled. Cumin or carraway seed is still used today in the preparation of the delicious “Bavarian” cabbage which also includes wine and other spices.",
      "categories": []
    },
    {
      "name": "Young Cabbage, Sprouts, Another Way",
      "photo_filename": null,
      "servings": null,
      "prep_time": null,
      "cook_time": null,
      "ingredients": [
        "STALKS",
        "LEAVES",
        "CORIANDER",
        "ONION",
        "CUMIN",
        "PEPPER",
        "RAISIN WINE",
        "CONDENSED WINE",
        "OIL"
      ],
      "directions": [
        "CUT THE STALKS IN HALF AND BOIL THEM. THE LEAVES ARE MASHED AND SEASONED WITH CORIANDER, ONION, CUMIN, PEPPER, RAISIN WINE, OR CONDENSED WINE AND A LITTLE OIL."
      ],
      "notes": "Very sensible way of using cabbage stalks that are usually thrown away. Note the almost scientific procedure: the stalks are separated from the leaves, split to facilitate cooking; they are cooked separately because they require more time than the tender greens. Our present method appears barbarous in comparison. We quarter the cabbage head, and either boil it or steam it. As a result either the tender leaves are cooked to death or the stems are still hard. The overcooked parts are not palatable, the underdone ones indigestible. Such being the case, our boiled cabbage is a complete loss, unless prepared the Apician way.",
      "categories": []
    },

    {
      "name": "Young Cabbage, Sprouts, Another Way (with Spelt and Pine Nuts)",
      "photo_filename": null,
      "servings": null,
      "prep_time": null,
      "cook_time": null,
      "ingredients": [
        "SPROUTS (prepared in the above way)",
        "BOILED SPELT",
        "PINE NUTS",
        "RAISINS"
      ],
      "directions": [
        "PREPARE THE SPROUTS IN THE ABOVE WAY, COVER THEM WITH BOILED SPELT AND PINE NUTS AND SPRINKLE WITH RAISINS."
      ],
      "notes": "The nuts should not astonish us. The French today have a delicious dish, Choux de Bruxelles aux Marrons—Brussels Sprouts with Chestnuts. Sprouts and chestnuts are, of course, cooked separately; the lightly boiled sprouts are sauté in butter; the chestnuts parboiled, peeled, and finished in stock with a little sugar or syrup, tossed in butter and served in the center of the sprouts. The Apician formula with cereal and raisins added is too exotic to suit our modern taste, but without a question is a nutritious dish and complete from a dietetic point of view.",
      "categories": []
    },
    {
      "name": "Leeks",
      "photo_filename": null,
      "servings": null,
      "prep_time": null,
      "cook_time": null,
      "ingredients": [

        "WELL MATURED LEEKS ARE BOILED WITH A PINCH OF SALT IN [combined] WATER AND OIL. THEY ARE THEN STEWED IN OIL AND IN THE BEST KIND OF BROTH, AND SERVED."
      ],
      "notes": "One of the rare instances where Apicius mentions salt in cookery, i.e., salt in a dry form. Pugnum salis—a fist of salt—he prescribes here. Usually it is liquamen—broth, brine—he uses.",

      "photo_filename": null,
      "servings": null,
      "prep_time": null,
      "cook_time": null,
      "ingredients": [
        "2 OUNCES OF GINGER",
        "1 OUNCE OF GREEN RUE",
        "1 OUNCE OF MEATY DATES",
        "12 SCRUPLES OF GROUND PEPPER",
        "1 OUNCE OF GOOD HONEY",
        "8 OUNCES OF EITHER ÆTHIOPIAN OR SYRIAN CUMIN",
        "VINEGAR",
        "STOCK"

      "directions": [
        "MAKE AN INFUSION OF THIS IN VINEGAR, THE CUMIN CRUSHED, AND STRAIN. OF THIS LIQUOR USE A SMALL SPOONFUL MIX IT WITH STOCK AND A LITTLE VINEGAR: YOU MAY TAKE A SMALL SPOONFUL AFTER THE MEAL."
      ],
      "notes": "This is another of the medical formulæ that have suffered much by experimentation and interpretation through the ages. It seems to be an aromatic vinegar for a salad dressing, and, as such, a very interesting article, reminding of our present tarragon, etc., vinegars. To be used judiciously in salads. Again, as might be expected, the medicinal character of the formula inspires the medieval doctors to profound meditation and lively debate.",
